stops.name: San Felipe de Neri Church
stops.teaser: A church that collapsed, got rebuilt in 1793, and has been in use ever since.
stops.map: San Felipe de Neri Church, 2005 N Plaza St NW, Albuquerque, NM
stops.clue: Go to Old Town and find the Plaza. On its north side, look for a church with a pair of pointed towers.
stops.safety: Old Town has narrow streets and lots of foot traffic. Use crosswalks, and be quiet if you step inside, since it is a place of worship.

q.hint: Look at the front from across the Plaza.

then.line: A postcard of the church with its two towers, soon after 1898.

now.head: Today
now.label: The church today

story: The church was founded in 1706 by Fray Manuel Moreno, one of the original settlers of Albuquerque. It was first dedicated to Saint Francis Xavier, but the Viceroy changed the patron saint to Saint Philip Neri in July 1706 to honor King Philip V.

The first church fell down in the winter of 1792 to 1793. The governor called the collapse a disgrace and ordered everyone nearby to help build a new one. Construction on the second church began in 1793.

Under Bishop Jean-Baptiste Lamy in the Victorian era, the church was remodeled with Gothic Revival bell towers and a pitched roof. It is the only building in Old Town proven to date to the Spanish colonial period, and it has been in use for over 200 years.
stops.fact: The first church fell down, and the town rebuilt it.
stops.disputed: Many people think the whole church is a single colonial building. Wikipedia says the Gothic bell towers and roof were added later, in the Victorian era.

claims.t: The current church was begun in 1793.
claims.why: Wikipedia: the new church was begun in 1793.

claims.t: The first church from 1706 is the one still standing.
claims.why: The first church collapsed in the winter of 1792 to 1793.

sources.t: Wikipedia: San Felipe de Neri Church

stops.name: Alvarado Hotel site
stops.teaser: The biggest Harvey House hotel ever, torn down in 1970.
stops.map: Alvarado Transportation Center, 100 1st St SW, Albuquerque, NM
stops.clue: Go to First Street downtown, by the train platforms. Look for the red-roofed station building with a tall tower.
stops.safety: This is a working train and bus center. Stay on public walkways, keep clear of the tracks, and watch for buses.

now.label: The site today

story: The Alvarado Hotel was built in 1901 and 1902 by the Santa Fe Railway and opened on May 10, 1902. The Fred Harvey Company ran it. Charles Frederick Whittlesey designed it in the Mission Revival style, and he also designed El Tovar at the Grand Canyon.

In 1922 it was remodeled and expanded to 120 rooms, with interiors redone by architect Mary Colter. It was then the largest of all the Harvey hotels, and for many travelers it was their first look at the American Southwest.

The railroad tore it down in 1970. A preservationist called it the most serious loss of a landmark the city had suffered, and it helped rally support for saving old buildings. The Alvarado Transportation Center opened on the site in 2002.
stops.fact: It was the biggest Harvey House ever built.
stops.disputed: The Alvarado Transportation Center is named for the lost hotel, but the hotel itself is gone. Wikipedia says the center stands on its site.

claims.t: The Alvarado Hotel is still standing.

stops.name: KiMo Theatre
stops.teaser: A movie palace named in a contest, and designed to look like a pueblo.
stops.map: KiMo Theatre, 423 Central Ave NW, Albuquerque, NM
stops.clue: Go to Central Avenue at 5th Street downtown. Look for the cream-colored building with colorful decorations and a tall red neon sign.
stops.safety: Central Avenue is busy. Use crosswalks, check box office hours, and keep off the street when taking photos.

story: The KiMo opened on September 19, 1927, in a style called Pueblo Deco, a blend of Pueblo Revival and Art Deco. The Boller Brothers architecture firm designed it, after studying Southwest cultures and building styles.

The Albuquerque Journal held a naming contest with a $50 prize. The name had to be Indian and could not have more than six letters. Pablo Abeita, a former governor of Isleta Pueblo, won with "Kimo", which means mountain lion.
The theater closed in 1970 and a fire damaged it by 1977. The family sold it to the city, which saved it and restored it. A replica of the original neon sign, 24 feet tall, went up in June 2011.
stops.fact: The theater's name came from a contest.
stops.disputed: Some people say Kimo means "king of the beasts". Wikipedia says it means mountain lion, sometimes loosely translated that way.

claims.t: The architect named the theater himself.
claims.why: Pablo Abeita won a newspaper naming contest.

stops.name: Santa Fe Railway Shops
stops.teaser: A railroad workshop so big that it was Albuquerque's biggest employer.
stops.map: Albuquerque Rail Yards, 777 1st St SW, Albuquerque, NM
stops.clue: Go south of downtown to the Barelas neighborhood. Look for a huge old industrial building with tall glass walls.
stops.safety: Much of the rail yard is private or closed. View from public streets, and do not enter fenced areas.

story: The Santa Fe Railway built shops in Albuquerque in the 1880s. The buildings that remain were put up between 1915 and 1925, and the shops became the city's biggest employer, with 970 workers in 1919 and a peak of 1,500 in the 1940s.
The main job was steam locomotive maintenance. Each locomotive needed a full rebuild every 12 to 18 months, and the shops finished about 40 overhauls a month at their peak.

The huge erection and machine shop was designed in 1920 and built in eight months, starting in February 1921. It covers about 165,000 square feet, with a main bay 604 feet long, 57 feet high and a crane that can lift 250 tons. Work declined in the 1950s as the railroad switched to diesel, and the shops later sat empty.
stops.fact: The main bay is 604 feet long.
stops.disputed: Many people think railroad shops like these built diesel locomotives. Wikipedia says the Santa Fe moved diesel repair to other yards.

claims.t: The shops were once Albuquerque's largest employer.
claims.why: Wikipedia: they were the largest employer in the city in their heyday.

claims.t: The shops mostly serviced diesel engines.
claims.why: Their core work was steam locomotive maintenance.
